description: The law of demand, why demand curves slope down, and the factors that shift demand versus a movement along it.
content_html:
What Is Demand?

In economics, demand does not simply mean wanting something. It means being both willing and able to buy it. A teenager who wants a new games console but has no money is not contributing to demand in the economic sense — there is no “effective demand” unless the desire is backed by the purchasing power to act on it. Economists focus on this distinction because markets respond to spending, not wishes.

Demand is always for a good or service at a particular price, over a particular time period. When economists talk about “the demand for petrol”, they mean the total quantity all consumers are willing and able to purchase at each possible price, holding all other factors constant. This set of price–quantity relationships is captured in a demand schedule and drawn as a demand curve.

The Law of Demand

The central rule of demand is the law of demand: as the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls. As the price falls, the quantity demanded rises. The relationship between price and quantity demanded is inverse — they move in opposite directions.

Think about the petrol market. When fuel prices spike to 170p a litre, many drivers combine journeys, take public transport more often, or walk short distances they would normally drive. Fewer litres are bought. When prices fall to 130p, the same drivers fill up more readily and make trips they previously avoided. The quantity demanded rises. This behaviour is consistent and predictable across virtually every market.

There are two reasons why demand behaves this way. First, as a good becomes more expensive it also becomes expensive relative to alternatives, so consumers switch to substitutes — this is the substitution effect. Second, a price rise reduces the real purchasing power of a consumer’s income, so they can afford to buy less overall — this is the income effect. Both effects push quantity demanded in the same direction: downwards when price rises.

Key Fact

The demand curve slopes downward from left to right because of the law of demand: higher prices reduce quantity demanded (substitution effect + income effect). A demand curve is drawn with price on the vertical axis and quantity demanded on the horizontal axis.

Movement Along the Demand Curve

A change in the price of the good itself causes a movement along the demand curve. If petrol rises from 140p to 160p per litre, consumers move up the demand curve to a lower quantity demanded. If it falls to 120p, they move down to a higher quantity. The curve itself does not move — only the position of the consumer on it changes.

It is important to use precise language here. A rise in price causes a contraction of demand — less is demanded. A fall in price causes an extension of demand — more is demanded. Examiners expect you to use these terms rather than simply saying demand “goes up” or “goes down” when the price changes.

Students frequently write that a price rise “decreases demand”. This is technically incorrect and can cost marks. When price changes, the demand curve stays fixed — only the quantity demanded changes, shown as a movement along the existing curve. The correct phrasing is: a price rise causes a contraction of demand (a fall in quantity demanded). A price fall causes an extension of demand (a rise in quantity demanded). Reserve the phrase “demand increases” or “demand decreases” for when the whole curve shifts due to a non-price factor.

Shifts in the Demand Curve

A shift in the demand curve happens when a factor other than price changes. The whole curve moves — at every possible price, consumers now want a different quantity. A rightward shift means more is demanded at every price; a leftward shift means less is demanded at every price. The factors that cause shifts are sometimes called the conditions of demand.

To picture this: imagine petrol demand before and after a 20% rise in household incomes. At every price point, drivers are now willing to buy more fuel — they take more car journeys, use the car for shorter trips, and are less sensitive to cost. The entire demand curve shifts to the right. Price has not changed; the conditions of demand have changed.

Key Fact

The main factors that shift the demand curve are: income, tastes and fashion, the prices of related goods, population and demographics, advertising, and interest rates or credit availability. A rightward shift shows a rise in demand; a leftward shift shows a fall in demand.

Factors That Shift Demand

Income. For most goods (called normal goods), a rise in income shifts the demand curve to the right. People buy more holidays, restaurant meals and new clothes when they earn more. For a small category of goods (called inferior goods), demand actually falls as income rises — for example, demand for budget own-brand foods tends to fall when incomes improve, as consumers trade up to branded alternatives.

Tastes and fashion. Consumer preferences change over time. The rise of plant-based diets shifted the demand curve for meat alternatives sharply to the right through the 2010s. Meanwhile, demand for physical DVDs shifted to the left as streaming services became dominant. Advertising and social media trends can accelerate these changes in taste rapidly.

Prices of related goods. Two goods can be related as substitutes or complements. If the price of bus fares rises sharply, demand for cars may increase — consumers switch from one mode of transport to the other. If the price of car insurance rises steeply, demand for cars themselves may fall, because the total cost of motoring has risen even though the car’s own price is unchanged.

Population. A larger population, or a change in its age structure, shifts demand. An ageing population, for instance, increases demand for healthcare, mobility aids and retirement housing. A rising number of young adults increases demand for rented accommodation and entry-level smartphones.

Advertising. Effective advertising changes consumer preferences, shifting the demand curve to the right for the advertised product. When a supermarket runs a major promotional campaign for its own-brand products, demand at every price point may rise.

The most common mistake in demand questions is confusing these two. Ask yourself: What has changed? If the answer is the good’s own price, you have a movement along the curve — either an extension (price falls, quantity demanded rises) or a contraction (price rises, quantity demanded falls). If the answer is anything else — income, tastes, prices of other goods, population, advertising — you have a shift of the whole curve. A rightward shift means demand has increased; a leftward shift means demand has decreased. Examiners mark this distinction very precisely.

A Worked Example

Consider the market for electric vehicles (EVs). Suppose manufacturers cut the price of a popular EV model from £35,000 to £28,000. The fall in the good’s own price causes an extension of demand — a movement down the demand curve to a higher quantity. This is a movement along the existing curve; the curve itself does not move. At the same time, a high-profile advertising campaign promotes the environmental benefits of EVs, changing consumer tastes in favour of them. This causes a rightward shift of the entire demand curve. Both changes increase the quantity of EVs demanded, but they work through different mechanisms and would be shown differently on a demand diagram: the price cut is a movement along the curve; the advertising campaign is a shift of the curve.
exam_tip_html: The command word Explain tells you to develop a chain of reasoning: state the factor, say how it affects consumers’ decisions, then state the outcome for quantity demanded and price. For example: “Consumer incomes rise → people can afford more at every price level → the demand curve shifts to the right → at the existing price, there is now excess demand → price is bid up.” A common error is writing that “demand increases” when price falls — that is an extension of demand (a movement along the curve), not a shift. Equally, writing that “demand decreases” when price rises is wrong — that is a contraction of demand. Save ‘demand increases’ or ‘demand decreases’ only for when the whole curve shifts due to a non-price factor.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The law of demand states that, all else equal, a rise in price leads to a fall in quantity demanded — shown as a downward-sloping demand curve with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis.
  • A change in the good’s own price causes a movement along the demand curve (extension if price falls, contraction if price rises) — not a shift.
  • Non-price factors — income, tastes and fashion, prices of related goods, population, advertising, and interest rates or credit availability — shift the whole demand curve right (demand rises) or left (demand falls).

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the law of demand?
A. As the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded rises.
B. As the price of a good falls, the quantity demanded falls.
C. As the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls.
D. As income rises, the price of a good falls.

A cinema ticket costs £12 and consumers buy 400 tickets per week. The cinema raises the price to £15. Using the data below, calculate the percentage change in quantity demanded.

Quantity demanded at £12: 400 tickets per week
Quantity demanded at £15: 300 tickets per week

Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the correct method: percentage change = ((300 − 400) ÷ 400) × 100; 1 mark for the correct answer of −25%.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a rise in consumer incomes is likely to increase the demand for restaurant meals.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that restaurant meals are a normal good; 1 mark for explaining that higher income means consumers have more purchasing power; 1 mark for developing the chain: greater purchasing power allows consumers to afford more restaurant meals at every price level, shifting the demand curve to the right.

practice_questions.text: A new government report recommends that people reduce their consumption of processed meat for health reasons. Using demand analysis, explain how this change in consumer tastes is likely to affect the market for plant-based meat alternatives.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the change in tastes as a non-price shift factor; 1 mark for explaining that demand for plant-based alternatives increases as consumers substitute away from processed meat; 1 mark for describing the rightward shift of the demand curve for plant-based products; 1 mark for explaining the consequence — at the existing price, there is excess demand, pushing the price of plant-based alternatives upward.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a significant fall in the price of electric vehicles (EVs) is likely to affect the quantity of EVs demanded and the market for petrol-powered cars.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Develops a full chain of reasoning for both markets. Explains the extension of demand in the EV market (movement along the demand curve, price falls → quantity demanded rises). Then analyses the cross-market effect: EVs and petrol cars are substitutes, so rising EV demand shifts the demand curve for petrol cars to the left, reducing both equilibrium price and quantity sold. Demonstrates understanding of movement vs shift distinction throughout.

Secure (3–4 marks): Correctly identifies the extension in EV demand and recognises that petrol cars are substitutes. Explains at least one cross-market effect with some development.

Developing (2 marks): Identifies that more EVs will be demanded and that this may affect petrol cars, but explanation is limited or incomplete.

Emerging (1 mark): Makes a simple relevant point, such as that a lower price increases demand for EVs, with no development.

practice_questions.text: "A rise in household incomes is always good news for producers in every market." Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): Presents a well-structured evaluation of both sides. For: rising incomes increase demand for normal goods (restaurants, holidays, electronics), shifting demand curves right and raising equilibrium price and quantity — boosting producer revenues. Against: for inferior goods (budget supermarket products, payday loans, low-cost clothing brands), rising incomes shift demand to the left, harming producers. Provides a supported judgement: the impact depends on the type of good — producers of normal goods benefit while producers of inferior goods face falling demand. May also note that rising incomes could push up input costs (higher wages), partly offsetting the revenue gain.

Secure (5–7 marks): Correctly explains benefits for producers of normal goods and acknowledges some producers may be harmed. Attempts a judgement.

Developing (3–4 marks): Identifies that higher incomes increase demand generally, with limited or one-sided analysis.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Makes a simple point that rising incomes are good for producers, with no development of exceptions or a judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: What does a rightward shift of the demand curve indicate?
options: A fall in the good's own price
A rise in the quantity demanded at every price level
A fall in the quantity demanded at every price level
A rise in the good's own price

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following would cause a contraction of demand rather than a fall in demand?
options: A change in consumer tastes away from the good
A rise in the price of the good itself

knowledge_checks.q: For most everyday goods, a rise in consumer incomes causes the demand curve to shift to the _____.
The law of demand states that, all other things being equal, as price rises, quantity demanded _____.
Match each term to its correct description.
right: Quantity demanded falls because the good's own price has risen
The whole curve moves because a non-price factor has changed
Quantity demanded rises because the good's own price has fallen

flashcard_questions.a: The quantity of a good consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price.
As price rises, quantity demanded falls; as price falls, quantity demanded rises.

flashcard_questions.q: What term describes a fall in quantity demanded caused by a rise in a good's own price?
flashcard_questions.a: A contraction of demand — a movement up the demand curve to a lower quantity.

flashcard_questions.q: What term describes a rise in quantity demanded caused by a fall in a good's own price?
flashcard_questions.a: An extension of demand — a movement down the demand curve to a higher quantity.

flashcard_questions.q: What term describes a good for which demand rises as consumer income rises?
Why does the demand curve slope downward? (Give the two effects.)
flashcard_questions.a: The substitution effect and the income effect both reduce quantity demanded when price rises.

flashcard_questions.q: Name six factors (conditions of demand) that shift the demand curve.
flashcard_questions.a: Income, tastes and fashion, prices of related goods, population, advertising, and interest rates or credit availability.

flashcard_questions.q: If a non-price factor increases demand, which direction does the demand curve shift?
What is the substitution effect of a price rise?
flashcard_questions.a: The good becomes more expensive relative to alternatives, so consumers switch to substitutes.

flashcard_questions.q: How does effective advertising affect the demand curve for a product?
flashcard_questions.a: It shifts the demand curve to the right — more is demanded at every price.
A good for which demand falls as consumer income rises.

flashcard_questions.q: Demand is only effective if the consumer is both _____ and _____ to buy.
On a demand curve diagram, price is on the _____ axis and quantity demanded is on the _____ axis.

glossary_terms.definition: The quantity of a good or service that consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price over a given time period.
A line on a price–quantity graph showing the quantity of a good consumers will buy at each price, assuming all other factors remain unchanged.
The principle that, all other things being equal, as the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls, and vice versa.
A change in quantity demanded caused solely by a change in the good's own price, represented by moving to a different point on the same demand curve.
A movement of the entire demand curve to a new position, caused by a change in any factor other than the good's own price.
A good for which demand rises as consumer income rises; the majority of everyday goods and services.
